focus: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding

items.title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
items.why: Speculative decoding is now a standard part of every serious inference stack, and the paper is a rare case where a systems speedup comes with a short, exact probabilistic proof. It trades spare compute for latency because decoding is memory-bound, and the speedup formula lets you reason about when it will or will not pay off.
items.summary:
Autoregressive decoding runs the large target model Mp once per token, and each step is memory-bound, so the hardware is underused. The idea: let a much cheaper approximation model Mq guess gamma tokens autoregressively, then run Mp once in parallel over the prefix and all guessed prefixes to get gamma+1 target distributions. Each iteration therefore yields between 1 and gamma+1 tokens for one target call.

The acceptance rule keeps the output distribution exactly equal to Mp's. A guessed token x drawn from q is accepted with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)). At the first rejection, the replacement token is sampled from the adjusted distribution norm(max(0, p - q)). If all gamma guesses pass, a bonus token is sampled from the target's final distribution. The appendix proves this is exactly p, so there is no quality trade-off, unlike distillation or quantization.

The math: define beta as the acceptance probability at a prefix and alpha as its expectation. alpha equals the expected sum over tokens of min(p, q), which is one minus the total variation distance between the two models. Under an i.i.d. assumption the expected tokens per iteration is (1 - alpha^(gamma+1)) / (1 - alpha), a geometric series capped at gamma+1. With cost coefficient c, the time ratio of one Mq call to one Mp call, the expected wall-time improvement is (1 - alpha^(gamma+1)) / ((1 - alpha)(gamma*c + 1)). A speedup exists only if alpha > c, and with a free draft model it is bounded by 1/(1 - alpha). You choose gamma by maximizing this numerically. The price is extra arithmetic: total operations rise by (1 - alpha)(gamma*c_hat + gamma + 1) / (1 - alpha^(gamma+1)), so it helps only when spare compute exists, such as small batches.

Experiments used T5-XXL (11B) as target with T5-small, base and large drafts on a single TPU-v4 at batch size 1, for WMT English-German translation and CNN/DM summarization. Speedups were 2.6x to 3.4x for translation and 2.3x to 3.1x for summarization depending on temperature, with T5-small as draft (alpha about 0.62 to 0.75, gamma 5 to 7). The larger T5-large draft was slower because its c is too high. Acceptance rates in other setups: about 0.74 to 0.75 for an 8B draft against LaMDA 137B, and only 0.03 to 0.23 for unigram or bigram drafts. Limits: fixed gamma, text only, and no help when compute is already saturated.
items.exercise: In Python with numpy, build two toy autoregressive models over a small vocabulary (for example a bigram table for q and a smoothed trigram table for p, or two small random-weight networks). Implement the speculative sampler exactly as described: sample gamma guesses, compute accept/reject with min(1, p/q), resample from norm(max(0, p - q)) on rejection, and add a bonus token when all pass. Verify empirically with a few hundred thousand samples that the first-token distribution matches p (chi-square test) even though you sample mostly from q. Then measure alpha and mean tokens per iteration, compare with the closed form (1 - alpha^(gamma+1)) / (1 - alpha), and plot the predicted speedup S over gamma for several values of c.

items.title: Write-Ahead Logging
items.why: SQLite WAL is the smallest complete example of a snapshot-reading, append-only commit protocol with checkpointing, and the same trade-offs (reader end marks, checkpoint starvation, WAL growth) appear in Postgres, RocksDB and every log-structured store. It is also the engine most likely to be embedded in anything you ship.
items.summary:
In the default rollback-journal mode, original pages are copied into a journal before the database file is modified, and commit means deleting the journal. WAL inverts this: the database file keeps the original content, changes are appended to a separate -wal file, and commit means appending a commit record. Many transactions can sit in one WAL.

Snapshot reads work through an end mark. When a read transaction starts, it records the position of the last valid commit record in the WAL. For each page it needs, it looks for the newest copy of that page before its end mark and falls back to the database file if there is none. A shared-memory structure called the wal-index, stored in the -shm file, makes that lookup fast without scanning the log. Different readers can hold different end marks, so each sees a consistent point-in-time snapshot while writers keep appending. Readers never block the writer and the writer never blocks readers, but there is a single WAL, so only one writer at a time.

Checkpointing copies committed pages from the WAL back into the database file. By default it triggers when a commit leaves the WAL at 1000 pages or more, and runs in the committing thread, so one commit in many is slow. A checkpoint cannot go past the end mark of any active reader, because it must not overwrite pages that reader still needs; it records progress and resumes later. The WAL must be synced before its content moves into the database and the database must be synced before the WAL is reused, so checkpoints are the expensive part. With synchronous=NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation that syncs, which is why commits become fast but are not durable across power loss.

Failure modes are instructive. Checkpoint starvation: if overlapping readers always keep at least one read transaction open, the WAL cannot be reset and grows without bound, so you need reader gaps or explicit RESTART or TRUNCATE checkpoints. The WAL is not truncated by default, only overwritten from the start, and journal_size_limit controls shrinking. The wal-index is a memory-mapped file (rarely over 32 KiB, never synced) because /dev/shm would break across chroots, which is also why all processes must share a host and network filesystems are unsupported. The page also documents a rare WAL-reset data race fixed in 3.51.3, a useful reminder that even the best-tested protocols have races.
items.exercise: With Python's sqlite3 module, set journal_mode=WAL and run one writer inserting in a loop plus several readers holding long-lived read transactions. Watch the -wal file size and PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE) results (busy, log, checkpointed pages) as you change reader behavior, and reproduce checkpoint starvation by always keeping one reader open. Then compare insert throughput and fsync counts (use strace -c or a counting VFS wrapper) for rollback journal, WAL with synchronous=FULL, and WAL with synchronous=NORMAL. Stretch: write a toy append-only store in C# or Python with an in-memory page index and reader end marks, and implement a passive checkpoint that stops at the minimum active end mark.

items.title: HyperLogLog in Practice: Algorithmic Engineering of a State of the Art Cardinality Estimation Algorithm
items.why: This is a masterclass in taking a clean theoretical sketch and engineering it: replacing an analytical correction with an empirical one, changing the hash width, and adding a compact sparse mode. It is the algorithm behind approximate distinct counts in BigQuery, Redis, Presto and Postgres extensions, and the probability behind it (order statistics of hash prefixes) is exactly the sort of math you can derive yourself.
items.summary:
Basic HyperLogLog hashes each element, uses the first p bits to pick one of m = 2^p registers, and stores in that register the maximum rho over the remaining bits, where rho is the position of the first one bit (leading zeros plus one). The raw estimate is a bias-corrected harmonic mean: E = alpha_m * m^2 / sum over registers of 2^(-M[j]), with alpha_m about 0.7213 / (1 + 1.079/m) for large m. Relative standard error is about 1.04 / sqrt(m), and memory is 5 bits per register with a 32-bit hash. The original paper patched the extremes: LinearCounting (m * ln(m / V), V being empty registers) for small cardinalities, and a log correction near 2^32.

The paper's engineering changes: first, use a 64-bit hash with 6-bit registers, which deletes the large-range correction entirely and pushes usable cardinalities past billions. Second, the transition region around 2.5m has a visible error spike because the raw estimator is biased there, so they measure the bias empirically: run thousands of random datasets per cardinality, record mean raw estimate minus truth, store about 200 interpolation points per precision, and at query time subtract a k-nearest-neighbor interpolated bias (k = 6) when E is below about 5m. They then pick LinearCounting or the bias-corrected estimate by an empirical threshold (around 11500 for p = 14), which removes the spike.

Third, a sparse representation for low cardinalities. Instead of allocating all 6 * 2^p bits, store (index, rho) pairs at a higher precision p' (default 25) so small sets get even lower error, and convert to the dense array once the list outgrows the dense size. Compression matters: for p = 14, a plain 32-bit pair costs 32 bits per element, varint encoding about 19.5, sorted difference encoding about 11.75, and folding rho into the hash-value encoding about 8.1, letting the sparse form hold about 12000 pairs before conversion. A temporary unsorted buffer is merged into the sorted compressed list at 25 percent of the maximum size. The paper reports up to 4x lower error in the sparse range, and uses the sketch for dictionary-size estimation in a column store with large memory savings.
items.exercise: In C# or Python, implement HyperLogLog with a 64-bit hash (xxHash or MurmurHash3), p = 14, and verify the 1.04/sqrt(m) error by running 1000 trials at cardinalities 10^2 to 10^7. Plot relative error and bias vs true cardinality for the raw estimator and observe the bump near 2.5m. Then build your own bias table by simulation (average raw estimate vs truth on a grid), add k-NN interpolation correction plus the LinearCounting switch, and show the bump disappears. Stretch: implement the sparse mode with sorted-delta varint encoding and measure bits per element, and test merge (register-wise max) on partitioned data.

items.title: Addressing Cascading Failures (Google SRE Book, Chapter 22)
items.source: Google SRE book, Mike Ulrich (ed. Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy)
items.why: Most large outages are cascades, not single faults, and the failure mechanics here (retry amplification, queue sizing, GC death spirals, deadline propagation) are the ones that hit any service graph, including a healthcare backend calling Azure or GCP dependencies. The chapter gives arithmetic you can use in design reviews to size queues, retry budgets and deadlines.
items.summary:
A cascading failure is positive feedback: one component failing raises the load and failure odds of the rest. The root is usually server overload. If cluster B fails and cluster A's load jumps from 1000 to 1200 QPS, A's successful throughput can drop below 1000, and a service that is stable at 10,000 QPS but crash-loops at 11,000 will not recover when load drops to 9,000, because a mostly unhealthy fleet must handle the same traffic. If only 10 percent of servers are healthy, load may need to fall to roughly 1,000 QPS before it stabilizes. Resource exhaustion paths include CPU (queues grow, health checks time out, RPCs miss deadlines so work is wasted), memory (more in-flight requests means more RAM and a GC death spiral where less CPU means more GC), threads, and file descriptors.

Prevention priorities: load test to find the breaking point and the failure mode, serve degraded results, reject early and cheaply at servers, load balancers and proxies, and plan capacity, though capacity alone is not enough. Queue management: a queue ten times the thread count at 100 ms handling time means about 1.1 seconds of latency when full, so for steady traffic keep queues around half the thread pool or smaller. Under overload, serve newest requests first (LIFO) or use CoDel-like policies, because a request that waited 10 seconds is probably abandoned by the user and serving it is wasted work.

Retries are a frequent cause. In the chapter's example, a backend limited to 10,000 QPS per task receives 10,100 QPS, and retries compound the load until the backend melts. Guidance: randomized exponential backoff, a cap on retries per request, a process-wide retry budget (for example 60 per minute), no stacked retries across layers (3 retries across 4 layers means 4^3 = 64 attempts at the database per user action), and distinguishing retriable from permanent errors.

Deadlines: propagate an absolute deadline down the RPC tree and check remaining time before each stage, subtracting a few hundred milliseconds for transit, and propagate cancellation. Bimodal latency example: with 10 servers of 100 threads, 1000 QPS and 100 ms normal latency, if 5 percent of requests hang to a 100-second deadline they occupy about 5000 threads and only about 20 percent of requests succeed. Fail fast and keep deadlines within an order of magnitude of normal latency. The remaining sections cover cold-cache startup, testing ramps and spikes, and emergency remedies; I read those through a summary rather than verbatim.
items.exercise: In Python with simpy (or a plain discrete-event loop), simulate a client tier calling a backend with a bounded thread pool and queue. Reproduce the retry meltdown: set backend capacity at 10,000 QPS-equivalent, offer slightly more, and give clients up to 3 immediate retries with no jitter. Show goodput collapsing and failing to recover after load returns to normal. Then add, one at a time, exponential backoff with jitter, a per-process retry budget, a small queue with LIFO plus deadline-based dropping, and load shedding at the server, and plot goodput and p99 latency against offered load for each variant. Report the offered load at which each configuration recovers from a 30-second overload spike.
